The Śākya school has lost its jewel;
the central pillar of heaven has snapped in two;
the ferryboat has suddenly capsized.
Vastly surging is the sea of suffering;
upon what can one rely?
When tears are exhausted, they are followed by blood.
My heart is crushed and my spirit is lost.
I, the junior Qian, have held the handkerchief, the staff, and the *śikya* for nine years now;
I have grasped the pen and held the inkstone for only eight years.
Having the honor of occupying a place among translators,
I have humbly inherited the traces of his profound and esoteric teachings.
As for the origins of the Great Master’s conduct and transformation of beings:
I personally received his instructions during his lifetime,
when he commanded me to compose this preface.
Being occupied with the duties of service,
I have had no leisure to compose and edit [this work];
how much less could I have fulfilled the final testament left behind at the moment of death?
Though he firmly declined, he could not prevail;
as death approached, his breath failed,
and his tears of grief were beyond restraint.
Of all the various stories [concerning this],
not one in ten can be relied upon.
I respectfully submit this report.

On the first day of the second month in the third year of Ōei, it was transcribed using a certain manuscript; it was subsequently collated and verified against an old manuscript from Hosshūin. Written by the Acting Junior Head of the Monastic Order, Kenpō, aged thirty-eight, in the forty-eighth year of the Enkyō era, the Year of the Hare (1747). Completed with eight revisions by the Archbishop, Kenga, at the age of sixty-four.
